title: Rogation days
hookLine: villages walk their boundaries praying for the crops

lines: FIELD TO FIELD, MARKER TO MARKER.
cards: A stone sits half sunk in a hedge at the edge of a field, its letters worn almost smooth. On a set day, in some English villages, a crowd turns up beside it: the priest, the farmers, children carrying long willow sticks.

They've walked since morning, field to field, stopping at every marker where their parish ends. At each one, someone reads, someone prays for the crops, and the children whack the stone so they'll remember where it is.
In the old stories, sometimes it was the children who got bumped on it. The custom has a blunt name: beating the bounds. The days it belongs to have a gentler one.

teach.b: Tradition explains the name from the Latin for asking, and asking is the whole point: rain at the right time, sun at the right time, a harvest, the things a village can't make for itself. Two old lines fit the day.

teach.h: THE EARTH SHALL YIELD HER INCREASE.
teach.b: A psalm, in the King James Bible: "Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us." And Jesus's plain invitation: "Ask, and it shall be given you."
A town that grows its own food knows how little of it is in human hands, and Rogation says so out loud, on foot, in the fields. Why walk the boundary?
Partly memory: the line lived in people's heads, so the young had to see the stones. But there's a moral edge too.
Deuteronomy says: "Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance." A boundary stone protects the person on the other side as much as you.
Walking it and praying at it says: this much is ours to tend, that much is our neighbor's, and we won't creep.
So beating the bounds holds two things together: asking God for enough, and honoring where enough ends.
Some churches still walk their parish, in the country or around city blocks, praying for the homes, shops and gardens they pass, and for the people who work the land everywhere.

how: On Rogation days some parishes walk their boundaries in procession, stopping at markers to read scripture and pray for the crops and the community; some city churches walk their streets instead.

games.q: you're walking the bounds with your parish. you reach the stone that marks where your land meets the next village's. what happens there?
o: hurry past: it's just a rock.
stop, read, pray, and make sure the youngest will remember the spot.
nudge it a little further out while nobody's looking.
games.why: the walkers stop at each marker to read and pray, and the children strike the stone so they'll remember it. moving it is exactly what Deuteronomy forbids.

practice: Start at your own front door and walk to the corner in your mind, picturing who lives along the way, the shop, the tree, the patch where something grows.
At each corner, stop: if you pray, ask for what that stretch needs, work, rest, food on the table, peace between the houses; if you don't, just wish each stretch well as you pass it.

wordCard.voice: Rogation days. Days of asking, when some parishes walk their boundaries, praying for the crops and for the people inside the line and beyond it.

orig.note: Hebrew: border, boundary. Deuteronomy uses it for a neighbor's landmark.

carryVoice: Your line: beating the bounds. A stone that guards your neighbor as much as you. Go gently.
